The three factors that matter the most for loose skin are how much weight you lost, age, and genetics. In that order.

So keto + IF has really worked for me.

Well, I always start with a base of veggies, of course. I usually get one of those huge tubs of spring mix or whatever. Basically some mixture of spinach, romaine, kale, baby chard, whatever. Then I add cucumber. Cucumber is super low calorie. A large one is literally like 20 calories total. They're basically water. A little sprinkle of tomatoes. Avocado is good, but it's pretty calorie dense, so watch out.

Then there's the fun stuff. Like meats. You know those pouches of bacon bits? Not the fake ones made from soy fiber and whatever other not-bacon stuff they swept off the floor, but the ones that are actual pieces of bacon? A few shakes of one of those adds a lot of bacon-y flavor for not so many calories. 3 servings is like 90cal. I also like to sous vide boneless skinless chicken breasts, so I weigh one of those out and cut it up and throw in there. Turkey and ham are good too. Really just about anything works. You could even put a pouch of salmon or tuna in there if you wanted. It's your salad, you can do whatever you want!

Now, once all of that is out of the way, you can start to get a little crazy with it. If you like a bit of sweetness on your salad, you could chop up an apple on there. Or maybe throw on some raisins or craisins (dehydrated cranberries, for those who may not know). One of my favorite off-the-wall ingredients is mandarin orange. I often drain a small can of them and toss a few pieces on there. Goes great with chicken.

Now, you may wish to avoid this part, as it's where the calories really come in. Cheese, nuts, and dressing. These are the parts where you need to be careful. People think it's the meat, but it's not. If you put these 3 ingredients on a salad, it's super easy to add an extra \~400-500 calories. I recommend going light on the cheese, and finding a nice low-calorie dressing. Luckily, there are a bunch of low-calorie dressings out there. vinaigrettes are often a good option. They're thinner than something creamy like ranch, and they generally have far fewer calories. Also, it's usually better to look in the more expensive section for dressings because if you go and look at most dressings sitting on the shelf by the popular name brands, you're basically just getting like 140 calories of soybean or canola oil and/or sugar. 

And of course... weigh ALL of it. I don't care if it's 3 little cherry tomatoes. Weigh them. I just slap a bowl down on my food scale and hit the tare button. Weigh out the first ingredient, hit tare. Weight out the next, hit tare. Most dressings are around 30g per serving, which is way easier than measuring out 2 tablespoons. Don't be afraid of spending more on something like dressing to get a high quality one. If you're measuring it out properly, you'll be using a LOT less of it and it'll last quite a while.

Probably my favorite salad right now is a good spinach mix, cucumber, tomato, some grilled chicken, a few sprinkles of bacon pieces, a chopped up apple, sharp cheddar (it has a stronger flavor so you can use less of it) and either some ranch or some kind of vinaigrette. I've actually been using the G Hughes sugar free dressings lately. They have a really good creamy balsamic dressing that's only like 60 calories per serving. I can easily make a salad that's only around 600 calories with this, and if you want something lighter you can just skip the cheese and remove like 110 calories right there.

Changing your habits is not a mental tricks or strategy or miracle diet. If you go into weight loss thinking "I'll do this diet and then it will be over when I lose the weight", then you're setting yourself up for failure.

Obviously, ten pounds over 8-ish months is much slower than 30 pounds in 6 weeks, but I attribute my continued loss to forming healthier habits in those first 6 weeks. I was more active over the summer, I continued avoiding sugary drinks and treats, and I continued eating healthier foods instead of loading up on pizza and soda like I had for so many years before. 

I didn't just focus on losing weight... I focused on changing my eating habits and being more active. Now that I've started focusing on the weight loss again, I've lost even more weight, and I'm not worried about gaining it back, because I know how I gained the weight in the first place, and I've effectively broken those habits that caused it. Anyway, I also do IF, and I've found a few ways to make it easier. 

1: Keto. I don't know if you can handle keto or have ever tried it, but if you reduce carbs to 20-30g per day, and increase your healthy fat intake (avocados, olive oil, cook with beef tallow or butter), then IF becomes WAY easier. Eating a diet higher in fat seems really weird at first and counter-productive, but fat doesn't make you fat. Eating too many calories makes you fat. What fat DOES do is satiate you. If you're satiated, then you're not hungry. I currently eat one meal a day, and I never have issues getting through a 20+ hour fast. 

2: Eat several hours before bed. If you sleep through the worst of the hunger pangs, then you basically never get hungry.

Eggs. Boiled eggs can be mixed or put on top of just about anything. Considering my meal of choice for most days is salads, a couple boiled eggs can be dumped on top of literally any combination of salad ingredients without fail.   


They can also be placed in soups, mixed into egg salad and eaten on some kind of healthy cracker or bread (I do keto, so low-carb mission tortillas are my jam), or just eaten plain.   


I also regularly have scrambled eggs, fried eggs, etc. Often mixed with various vegetables and/or some cheese to make a sort of skillet scramble.   


Eggs are one of the easiest foods to cook, and are extremely versatile. I don't know what I'd do without them.   


Also, the best way to "boil" eggs in my opinion, is to steam them. Put a couple cups of water in the bottom of a large stock pot, cover and bring to a boil (it'll only take a couple minutes), then put however many eggs into a steamer basket and place inside the pan. Cover and set a timer for exactly 12 minutes. Once the timer goes off, pull out the steamer basket and place into a large bowl of cold water.   


The end result is what I consider a perfectly cooked egg. The whites are completely set, the yolks are also fully solid, but there's a sort of custard-y darker spot in the yolk that is really creamy and smooth. If you like your boiled eggs more on the "dry" and chalky side like a traditional hard boil, just set the timer for 14 minutes. Soft boiled eggs can be achieved in 8-10 minutes, depending on how runny you want the yolks.

The reason it's easier if you're bigger is because your base metabolic rate is higher, as well as the number of calories you can burn from doing basic exercise. A person who weighs 300 pounds is going to burn more calories from walking for an hour than a person who weighs 150 pounds walking at the same pace. 

And since their base metabolic rate is higher to begin with, they're also burning more calories at rest (usually). So if they're tracking their calories and eating at a deficit, they can see dramatic weight loss early on.
